posts.quote: ONE HAYRIDE AND YOU WERE FINDING STRAW IN YOUR SOCKS UNTIL THANKSGIVING.
posts.caption: Every October the church or the 4-H or somebody's uncle with a tractor put together a hayride. You piled onto a flatbed wagon full of loose bales with every kid you knew, wrapped in a scratchy wool blanket that smelled like the cedar chest. The tractor never went faster than a walk, and somehow it still felt like an adventure. Somebody always started a hay fight, somebody always ended up with a fistful down their collar, and the grownups pretended not to notice. Afterward there was hot cider in paper cups and a bonfire you could feel on your face. And for weeks you'd pull off a sock and find another little piece of that night.
posts.first: Our hayrides went out past the Hendersons' back pasture and around the pond, and the tractor always stalled once, right at the spookiest part. I'm convinced Mr. Henderson did it on purpose. Best ten minutes of the whole fall.

posts.quote: THE BOWLING ALLEY HAD RENTED SHOES, PENCIL SCORECARDS, AND A SMELL YOU NEVER FORGOT.
posts.caption: Friday night was league night, Saturday morning was for the junior bowlers, and every birthday party in town landed somewhere in between. You walked up to the counter, said your size, and the man slid a pair of two-tone shoes across like he was handing over a prize. Somebody kept score with a stubby pencil, doing strike-and-spare math in their head faster than any machine. The pins crashed, the ball return rumbled, and the snack bar fried something all night long. That mix of lane oil, floor wax and french fries got into your coat and stayed there for a week. Nobody minded one bit.
posts.first: My dad bowled in a Thursday league for about thirty years and kept his own ball in a leather bag in the hall closet. Nobody was allowed to touch it. I'm pretty sure it weighed more than I did.

posts.quote: MOM COULD HEAR THE COOKIE JAR LID FROM THREE ROOMS AWAY.
posts.caption: You waited until she was busy. Ironing, on the phone, out back pinning laundry, it didn't matter. You dragged the step stool over without a sound, climbed up like a cat burglar, and lifted that lid as slow as any human being has ever lifted anything. And from somewhere in the back of the house came the voice: "You'll spoil your supper." Nobody ever figured out how she did it. That lid made a sound only mothers could hear.
posts.first: Our cookie jar was a ceramic owl, and its head was the lid. It had a little chip on one ear and rattled no matter how careful you were. I still think Mom picked it out for exactly that reason.

posts.quote: Dad fixed everything with duct tape, baling wire, and a few words we weren't allowed to repeat.
posts.first: My father kept a coffee can in the garage full of screws, washers and bolts from things that were long gone. Whatever broke, the answer was in that can somewhere. It took him an hour to find it, but it was always in there.

posts.quote: THE SLIDE RULE / BEFORE POCKET CALCULATORS, THE SMARTEST KID IN CLASS CARRIED ONE IN HIS SHIRT POCKET
posts.caption: Before anybody had a calculator, math class came with a stick that slid in the middle and had about a thousand tiny lines on it. The teacher kept a giant one hanging over the chalkboard, six feet long, so the whole class could follow along. If you knew how to read it, you could multiply, divide and find square roots without touching a pencil. Most of us never quite got there. But there was always one kid who did, and he carried his slide rule in a leather case like a sheriff wears a badge. Last I heard, he was building bridges.
posts.first: I got about as far as multiplying two numbers, as long as one of them was ten. My buddy Ray could do it in his sleep. I copied off Ray more than I care to admit.

posts.quote: DAD STOPPED AT EVERY HISTORICAL MARKER BETWEEN OUR HOUSE AND GRANDMA'S.
posts.caption: It didn't matter if we'd driven that road fifty times. If there was a little metal sign on a post by the side of the highway, the brakes came on. Dad got out, put his hands in his pockets, and read every word out loud like it was the Gettysburg Address. Something about a mill that burned down in 1871. Something about a man who slept here once. The rest of us sat in a hot car with the windows down, watching the cows watch us. It added two hours to every trip to Grandma's, and I'd give a lot to sit through one more.
posts.first: My dad kept a little spiral notebook in the glove box and wrote down every marker he ever read, with the date. Years later we found three of them full. My sister still keeps them on her bookshelf.

posts.quote: GRANDMA'S CAST IRON SKILLET NEVER SAW A DROP OF SOAP, AND NOTHING EVER STUCK TO IT.
posts.caption: Every kitchen had one, and it was older than anybody in the house. Black as a coal bucket, heavy enough to stop a burglar, and seasoned by forty years of bacon and cornbread. You did not put that skillet in the dishwater. You wiped it out, set it on the burner to dry, and rubbed a little grease into it like you were oiling a saddle. Eggs slid right off, and the cornbread came out with a crust you could knock on. When Grandma was gone, that skillet was the first thing anybody asked about.
posts.first: My grandmother's skillet hung on a nail by the stove, and she could tell from across the room if somebody had used soap on it. A cousin of mine scrubbed it with steel wool once. Grandma didn't speak to her until Easter.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the family doctor)
posts.quote: THE DOCTOR CAME TO THE HOUSE WITH A BLACK BAG, AND MOM MADE THE BEDS BEFORE HE GOT THERE.
posts.caption: If you were sick enough, the doctor came to you. He'd pull up in a dark sedan and come in with his hat in his hand and that black leather bag that seemed to hold everything. Before he arrived, the house got cleaned like the preacher was coming, sick kid or not. He'd sit on the edge of the bed, put a cold stethoscope on your chest, look down your throat with a flat wooden stick, and tell your mother to keep you in bed with plenty of fluids. Sometimes he stayed for a cup of coffee in the kitchen. You felt better the minute he walked in, and nobody could ever explain why.
posts.first: Our doctor delivered me, my brother, and half the kids in my class. He always had a peppermint in his coat pocket for whoever was sick. I think that peppermint did more good than the medicine.

posts.quote: Supper was at 5:30. Not 5:31. If you were late, you ate it cold and you ate it quiet.
posts.first: Mom rang a bell off the back porch, and every kid in the neighborhood knew whose bell was whose. You didn't finish the inning. You ran.

posts.character: Childhood rules and rituals (school picture day)
posts.quote: SCHOOL PICTURE DAY / MOM SLICKED YOUR HAIR DOWN WITH A WET COMB, AND IT POPPED BACK UP BEFORE THE BUS CAME
posts.caption: Picture day was the one morning a year your mother treated your head like a lawn that needed mowing. Out came the good shirt, the one with the collar that scratched. Then the comb went under the faucet, and she went after that cowlick like she was settling a score. It lay flat for maybe four minutes. By the time you sat on that little stool in the gym and the photographer said "big smile," it was standing straight up again. In every school picture we ever took, you can see that one piece of hair waving hello.
posts.first: My mother tried a dab of Dad's hair tonic on my cowlick one year. It didn't hold, and it made my hair shine like a bowling ball in the picture. That one hung in the hallway for twenty years.
